notes.meaning: David confronts corrupt judges and leaders who were supposed to defend the truth. Instead of protecting the innocent, they stayed silent or gave unfair rulings to please wicked rulers. David reminds them that they are merely mortal men who must one day answer to God.

These corrupt rulers do not just stumble into sin; they plan out evil deep in their hearts. They pretend to hold the scales of justice, but what they actually weigh out and hand to the people is cruelty and violence. Their public actions simply carry out the evil schemes they planned in secret.

Evil habits show up very early in life because human nature has been broken from the start. Sinners turn away from God and start telling lies as soon as they are able to speak. Their wrongdoing is not an accident, but the natural fruit of a corrupt heart.

differ.view: This verse teaches original sin and total depravity, meaning that all people inherit a sinful nature from birth.
This description is poetic exaggeration about especially corrupt men rather than a strict doctrinal statement about every infant at birth.

notes.meaning: The slander and evil words of these leaders act like deadly snake venom spreading through society. They are also compared to an adder that deliberately refuses to listen to the charmer's music. No wise reasoning, loving appeal, or warning from God can persuade them to change their stubborn ways.

David asks God to strip these oppressors of their power to hurt others, like knocking out the fangs of a snake or the teeth of a young lion. When their weapons of slander and violence are taken away, they can no longer tear their victims apart. The prayer asks God to disarm the bullies rather than take personal revenge.

The psalmist prays that the wicked will vanish like water soaking into desert sand, gone without a trace. When they pull back their bows to shoot at the innocent, he asks that their arrows snap or turn out blunt and useless. God is able to make their most dangerous plots completely fail.

Two vivid word pictures describe the total collapse of the wicked. Like a slug that seems to melt away into its own slime as it crawls, their own sinful lives will wear them out to nothing. Like a child stillborn in the dark, they will never live to enjoy the plans they made under the sun.

Judgment will strike the wicked far quicker than a cooking pot can feel the flame of burning thorn bushes. Before their schemes can cook or bring any results, God will sweep everything away like a sudden desert whirlwind. Their lives and their evil plans will be blown away in a single instant.

God's people will feel deep relief and joy when they see God put an end to oppression and set things right. Washing feet in the blood of the wicked is a battle picture showing total victory over enemies who seemed unbeatable. The joy is not a spiteful grudge, but pure praise that God's justice and holiness have won the day.

differ.view: Expressions that celebrate bloodshed belong to the older covenant and are completely foreign to the forgiving spirit Jesus calls Christians to live by.
Believers rightly rejoice in God's holy vengeance because it vindicates His justice, fulfills His promises, and delivers His church.

notes.meaning: When God finally steps in, all people will clearly see that serving the Lord is never in vain. Even onlookers will admit that a righteous life brings real reward and that the world is ruled by a living, just God. Divine justice removes all doubts and proves that evil never gets the last word.
